title: Science & Data for Readers
description: Develop the advanced reading and analytical skills needed to engage with scientific texts, data visualisations, and academic research. Covers the language of scientific reasoning, evaluating sources, interpreting statistics, and writing evidence-based arguments. Designed for C1 learners in STEM or research-adjacent fields.

questions.text: Two variables are correlated. Does this mean one causes the other?
options: No — correlation does not imply causation
Only if the study is peer-reviewed

Instead, it uses hedging language to express degrees of certainty and avoid overgeneralisation."}},{"id":"hD4eE5fF6g","type":"header","data":{"text":"Hedging Devices","level":3}},{"id":"hG7hH8iI9j","type":"list","data":{"style":"unordered","items":["Modal verbs: may, might, could, should, would","Epistemic adverbs: possibly, probably, arguably, apparently, seemingly","Verb phrases: seems to / tends to / appears to / is likely to","Approximators: approximately, around, roughly, up to","Limiting expressions: in most cases, under certain conditions, to some extent"]}},{"id":"hJ0kK1lL2m","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Compare:
❌ 'Social media causes depression.' (too strong — unhedged)
✅ 'The evidence suggests that heavy social media use may be associated with increased rates of depression in adolescents.' (hedged)"}}],"version":"2.31.4"}

content.text: The results ___ suggest that the intervention had a positive effect on cognitive performance. Participants ___ showed improved scores, although this ___ be due to practice effects rather than the treatment itself. The findings ___ need to be replicated in larger samples.

questions.text: Why do scientists use hedging language?
options: To make texts harder to understand
To avoid making claims that go beyond what the evidence supports

content.content: {"time":1700110004000,"blocks":[{"id":"evA1bB2cC3d","type":"paragraph","data":{"text":"Not all sources are equally reliable. Critical readers evaluate sources based on methodology, sample quality, potential bias, and reproducibility."}},{"id":"evD4eE5fF6g","type":"header","data":{"text":"Questions to Ask When Evaluating a Source","level":3}},{"id":"evG7hH8iI9j","type":"list","data":{"style":"unordered","items":["Who conducted the study? — Academic institution or commercial sponsor?","What was the sample size? — Small samples are less reliable.","Was there a control group? — Essential for establishing causation.","Has it been peer-reviewed? — Peer-reviewed journals have higher credibility.","Has it been replicated? — One study is not enough to establish a fact.","Could there be confounding variables? — Other factors that could explain the results."]}},{"id":"evJ0kK1lL2m","type":"header","data":{"text":"Language for Critical Evaluation","level":3}},{"id":"evM3nN4oO5p","type":"list","data":{"style":"unordered","items":["A significant limitation of this study is...","The findings must be interpreted with caution because...","The study suffers from a relatively small sample size.","Potential confounding variables include...","Further research is needed to establish whether..."]}}],"version":"2.31.4"}

questions.text: A study has a sample size of 12 people. What is the main concern?
options: Small samples reduce the reliability and generalisability of results
It hasn't been translated into English
A variable that the researcher controls
An uncontrolled factor that could influence the results
